title: Local polarization control of optical tweezer arrays
authors: Xiangkai Sun, Richard Bing-Shiun Tsai, Andrew Winnicki, Yuan Le, Kon H. Leung, Nelson Darkwah Oppong, Manuel Endres
abstract: Optical tweezer arrays trapping ultracold atoms and molecules are a versatile quantum science platform with broad impact in quantum simulation, quantum computation, and quantum metrology. The polarization dependence of anisotropic vector and tensor light shifts offers a degree of freedom for precise quantum state engineering of trapped particles. Similarly, state-selective operations depend on the polarization of the addressing light through the atom--light coupling strength. Yet, methods for controlling the polarization of individual tweezers or local addressing beams remain an experimental challenge. Here, we demonstrate independent, site-resolved linear polarization rotation across an optical tweezer array by exploiting the local birefringence tunability of a spatial light modulator. Applying this capability to an array of $^{88}\rm{Sr}$ atoms, we homogenize differential light shifts imparted by the 813-nm tweezers to the narrow ${^1{\rm S}_0}\leftrightarrow{^3{\rm P}_1}$ transition, enabling sideband cooling under a magic-angle condition. Furthermore, we show dynamic transport of trapped atoms across distinct polarization zones with high survival and preserved coherence. Finally, we characterize tweezer polarization noise and demonstrate closed-loop stabilization referenced to the atomic transition frequency, reaching mrad-level stability. Our work establishes a technique for manipulating polarization-sensitive atomic and molecular transitions in tweezer architectures, with immediate applications to optical tweezer clocks and multi-zone quantum processors.
summary: This paper presents a novel technique to independently control the polarization of light at every site within an optical tweezer array using a spatial light modulator. By achieving this site-resolved polarization control, the researchers successfully homogenized light shifts on trapped strontium atoms, enabling high-fidelity sideband cooling and controlled transport across the array. This technique is vital for building scalable, multi-zone quantum processors.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is achieving independent, site-resolved control over the polarization of individual optical tweezers within an array, which is necessary for advanced quantum state engineering.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated site-resolved linear polarization rotation using a spatial light modulator, enabling sideband cooling under a magic-angle condition and dynamic atom transport across polarization zones.
method: They exploit the local birefringence tunability of a liquid-crystal spatial light modulator (SLM) to imprint controlled phase retardations, thereby rotating the polarization at each trapping site.
model_or_system: The experiment uses optical tweezer arrays trapping ultracold strontium atoms ($^{88}	ext{Sr}$). The system relies on the polarization dependence of light shifts on atomic transitions, specifically the ${^1	ext{S}_0}\leftrightarrow{^3	ext{P}_1}$ intercombination line.

main_assumptions: The method assumes that the polarization-dependent light shift can be accurately mapped to the local birefringence tunability of the SLM.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup for local polarization control using the SLM, the tuning of the tensor light shift, the application of local polarization correction for efficient sideband cooling, and the programming of various polarization patterns for sequential operations.
paper_structure: The work progresses from establishing the fundamental technique of site-resolved polarization control to applying this control to homogenize light shifts for sideband cooling, demonstrating dynamic transport, and finally characterizing the stability of the polarization control system.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial experimental tool—local polarization control—that directly addresses a major bottleneck in scaling up quantum simulation and quantum computing architectures based on optical tweezers.
